description: Solo team building Medistra: a web app that shows which medical problems have no signed plan before a crew is out of reach of Earth. Live at https://medistra.vercel.app
summary: Medistra is for a crew member on a Mars surface stay who is not a doctor and must decide, when something goes wrong, whether to act now or wait for Earth. On the space station Earth answers in under a second. At Mars a question and its answer take 11 to 42 minutes, and about every two years NASA pauses commands to Mars for about two weeks while the Sun is in the way. Medistra compares how soon each of 72 conditions on NASA's lists needs a doctor with how long Earth takes to reply, and shows which have no signed order that lets the crew act first. For Mars on any day the verdict is "ORDERS: NO-GO, 7 missing". In a demo role the flight surgeon signs the missing orders in advance and the verdict turns. A daily check-in against NASA limits and a "Report a problem" screen complete it. It is a planning aid, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

  • Board. One verdict for the mission: "ORDERS: GO" or "ORDERS: NO-GO, 7 missing", always with "Checks the plan, not your health." A 3D figure marks the body areas with no signed order. A chart sets how soon a doctor is wanted against Earth's reply time.
  • Mission line. Space station, Moon and Mars, with NASA photographs, plus a "Sun between Earth and Mars" switch. Missing orders: station 0, Moon 0, Mars any day 7 (3 partly covered by an old NASA procedure), Mars with the Sun in the way 16.
  • Report a problem. Press a body area or search NASA's list. The answer says whether a signed order covers it and who acts now. Reports go into a mission log. It never diagnoses.
  • Check-in. Sleep, hours awake, work hours, exercise and cabin carbon dioxide, each held against a cited limit (for example NASA's 3 mmHg one-hour carbon dioxide limit). Vital signs are scored with NEWS2 only when all seven are entered. Tiredness, mood and stress are private and never set a status. Trend lines are labelled as forecasts.
  • Orders. Switch to "Flight surgeon (demo)", sign a draft order, and the count falls.
  • Sources. Every number has a "Why?" with its source and the quoted passage: 30 documents (4 not NASA's) and 26 stated assumptions.
  • Light and dark themes; works on phones.

How it works

A deterministic engine in TypeScript. The 72 conditions are NASA's 48 expected conditions (NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C, Table E.2-1) plus 24 high-consequence conditions from Table E.2-2 for which we found an urgency source. Reply times are round-trip light time from NASA JPL Horizons for 2026 to 2030; "Mars, any day" uses the shortest (10.77 minutes), so a gap there is a gap on every day. A condition is a gap when it needs a doctor sooner than Earth can reply and no procedure in NASA's 2001 ISS or 2006 Shuttle medical checklists, and no signed order, lets the crew act first. No AI model decides any status, verdict or escalation. Every limit and rule is data with a citation, and tests check each boundary.

How it covers the challenge

1. Gather: typed readings, sliders, and pressing the figure.

2. Evaluate: the verdict and the check-in's "need action" line.

3. Act: each item names who acts and what to do next; signed orders let the crew act first.

4. Visual: the figure, mission line, urgency chart and trends; status is never colour alone.

5. HRP hazards: every condition, order and check-in item is filed under one of the five hazards (our mapping). Radiation enters through NASA design requirements on Orders; there is no radiation reading in the check-in.

6. Escalation: crew member, crew medical officer or flight surgeon, with Earth's reply time shown.

7. Simple words: one question per screen, detail behind "Why?".

Limits

  • Not a medical device. The crew member is made up, and the draft orders were written for this demo; no physician wrote, signed or reviewed them.
  • The count is our calculation on NASA's lists, not NASA's. 4 to 7 conditions lack an order on a Mars day, depending on whether partly covered ones count.
  • For 5 of those 7, urgency comes from emergency-department waiting-time targets, not NASA.
  • Light time only: real replies are slower, so the counts are a floor.
  • The covering procedures date from 2001 and 2006 and are not current guidance.
  • The two-week pause applies to NASA's robotic Mars missions; applying it to a crew is our assumption.

Built at the event

Research began Sat 14 Nov 12:30 SGT; the first commit was 18:06. All code, data cleaning, the gap calculation, the tests and the live site were made on 14 and 15 November 2026.

Tools

TypeScript, React 19, Vite, three.js, Vitest (1,341 unit tests) and Playwright (850 end-to-end tests), hosted on Vercel. Our code is released under the Apache License 2.0.

Use of SI (Super Intelligence)

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used throughout. During the event it researched NASA sources, downloaded and analysed public NASA data, audited every claim, quote and licence, wrote the app's code, tests and data-cleaning scripts, drafted the text, and ran independent design reviews and a security audit.

Higgsfield made two assets on 15 Nov: the 3D human figure on the Board (Meshy 6 Text to 3D, geometry only, then reduced by our own script) and the spacecraft picture on the mission line and intro (GPT Image, background removed with Higgsfield's remover). Neither shows a real person, logo, flag, text or mission name.

The demo video is a real screen recording of the live app. Its voice-over (Seed Audio 1.0, a stock voice, not a real person's) and background music (ElevenLabs Music v2) were generated with Higgsfield; the video says so in its corner mark and in the file's metadata.

How it is labelled in the app: the figure carries the words "SI-generated figure." and the spacecraft "Spacecraft picture: SI-generated." wherever they appear; the Sources screen lists both as "Made with SI"; every source file carries an "SI-assisted code (Claude, Anthropic)" note. A full log is kept in SI_USAGE.md in the repository.
